title: HIPAA vs GDPR: how do their workforce training duties differ?
description: HIPAA names workforce privacy and security training as explicit duties with six year records; the GDPR requires training indirectly through accountability.
shortAnswer: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) states training duties outright: covered entities must train every workforce member on privacy policies and run a security awareness and training program, keeping documentation for six years. The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has no general training article. Training follows from its accountability, security and instruction duties, and from the data protection officer's task of monitoring staff awareness and training.
keyTakeaways: HIPAA has two explicit training standards: the Privacy Rule at 45 CFR 164.530(b) and the Security Rule at 45 CFR 164.308(a)(5).
The GDPR reaches training indirectly, through Articles 5(2), 24, 29 and 32(4), and names it directly only for the data protection officer (Article 39) and binding corporate rules (Article 47).
Neither law currently fixes an annual training cycle; a January 2025 HIPAA proposal would add one for security awareness training.
HIPAA sets a six year documentation retention rule; the GDPR sets none for training but requires the controller to be able to demonstrate compliance.
HIPAA applies by sector (health plans, clearinghouses, certain providers and their business associates); the GDPR applies to most processing of personal data in or targeting the EU.

sections.heading: What is the core difference between HIPAA and GDPR training duties?

blocks.text: The core difference is explicitness. HIPAA writes training into its rules as named standards with timing and documentation requirements. The GDPR leaves training implicit: an organization trains staff because it cannot otherwise show that its measures are appropriate and that people process data only on instructions.

Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, [45 CFR 164.530(b)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-E/section-164.530) requires a covered entity to train all members of its workforce on its policies and procedures for protected health information, as necessary and appropriate for their functions. New workforce members must be trained within a reasonable period after joining, staff affected by a material policy change within a reasonable period after it takes effect, and the training must be documented. The Security Rule at [45 CFR 164.308(a)(5)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-C/section-164.308) separately requires a security awareness and training program for all workforce members, including management.

The [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02016R0679-20160504) contains no clause telling controllers to train every employee. Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible for, and able to demonstrate, compliance; Article 24 requires appropriate technical and organizational measures; Articles 29 and 32(4) require that people acting under the controller's or processor's authority process personal data only on instructions. Article 39(1)(b) gives the data protection officer the task of monitoring compliance, including awareness raising and training of staff. Detail is on [GDPR staff training requirements](/regulations/gdpr-staff-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How do the security training expectations compare?

blocks.text: HIPAA lists security training topics; the GDPR leaves them to the controller's risk assessment. In practice both point toward role based training tied to the organization's actual controls.

The four HIPAA security training specifications are addressable, not optional. Under [45 CFR 164.306(d)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-C/section-164.306), an addressable specification must be implemented if reasonable and appropriate, or the entity must document why not and adopt an equivalent alternative where reasonable. A January 2025 [proposed rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/06/2024-30983/hipaa-security-rule-to-strengthen-the-cybersecurity-of-electronic-protected-health-information) would make security awareness training required at least once every 12 months, within 30 days of a new member gaining access and within 30 days of a material change. It is a proposal, so check the Federal Register for its status before building to it.

Article 32 of the GDPR requires security appropriate to the risk, and Article 32(4) requires steps to ensure that anyone with access processes data only on instructions. The European Data Protection Board's [guide for small business](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/sme-data-protection-guide/secure-personal-data_en) describes making employees aware of risks, measures and consequences, with information security training and periodic reminders. Because Article 32 sits in the Article 83(4) fine band, a security failure linked to untrained staff is an enforceable gap.

blocks.title: Practical consequence
blocks.text: A HIPAA auditor will usually ask to see the training documentation for a named workforce member. A GDPR supervisory authority will usually ask how the organization knows its measures, including training, are appropriate to the risk. Keep records that answer both: who was trained, on what, when, and how understanding was checked.

HIPAA applies because of what an organization is: a covered entity or business associate under US law. The GDPR applies because of where processing happens or whose data is processed. Many health and life sciences groups fall under both for different activities.

items: **US health plans, clearinghouses and providers that conduct standard electronic transactions:** HIPAA applies to protected health information. Business associates are covered by the Security Rule and by their contracts. See [HIPAA security and privacy training](/regulations/hipaa-security-and-privacy-training).
**Organizations established in the EU:** the GDPR applies to their processing of personal data, including health data of patients, trial participants and employees.

**US organizations without an EU establishment:** the GDPR can still apply under Article 3(2) if they offer goods or services to, or monitor the behavior of, people in the EU. This needs a case by case assessment.

**Groups with both:** for example, a US provider with an EU research subsidiary. Run one privacy and security curriculum with jurisdiction modules, and map each role to the rules that reach it. The [data privacy training requirements by country](/compare/data-privacy-training-requirements-by-country) comparison covers other markets.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each HIPAA standard and GDPR article as a separate obligation with provenance to the source text, then links roles, learning outcomes and assessment points to them before content is written. One curriculum can carry both laws, and the evidence shows which obligation each record satisfies.

faqs.a: Not in the current rule text. The Privacy Rule requires training within a reasonable period of joining and after material policy changes, and the Security Rule requires an ongoing awareness and training program without fixing a cycle. A January 2025 proposed rule would require security awareness training at least every 12 months, but a proposal is not binding until finalized.

faqs.q: Does the GDPR require a data protection officer to deliver training?
faqs.a: No. Article 39(1)(b) makes monitoring compliance, including awareness raising and training of staff, one of the officer's tasks. The officer oversees training and the related audits; delivery can sit with HR, learning or security teams. Article 37 sets the three cases in which an officer must be appointed.

faqs.q: Is HIPAA training enough for GDPR compliance?
faqs.a: Rarely on its own. HIPAA training covers protected health information and the entity's own policies. GDPR training must cover all personal data the role touches, data subject rights, lawful bases and the organization's EU specific procedures. Reuse the security content and add GDPR modules.

faqs.q: How long should training records be kept to satisfy both laws?
faqs.a: HIPAA requires documentation to be retained for six years from creation or the date it was last in effect. The GDPR sets no training specific period, but the controller must be able to demonstrate compliance. Keeping training records for at least six years covers HIPAA; see [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records) for other regimes.
